blocks.content: J&K's judicial history is intertwined with its constitutional status changes — this short but important chapter clarifies how the region's court system evolved from the old state-era arrangement to today's combined UT structure.
The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh serves as the common High Court for both Union Territories.
The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 facilitated the complete legal transition and application of Central Laws.
Local legal codes such as the Ranbir Penal Code (RPC) were replaced by standard Indian legal codes (IPC/BNS).
The judicial framework operates through two seasonal capitals, sitting at Srinagar and Jammu.

blocks.content: Under the old state-era Constitution, J&K had its own High Court (the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir), functioning under both the state's own Constitution and the applicable provisions of the Indian Constitution, with the Supreme Court of India as the ultimate court of appeal in matters governed by Indian constitutional/central law.

Following the 2019 reorganisation, the erstwhile High Court was renamed and its jurisdiction extended to cover both new Union Territories — it is now formally known as the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, with principal seats at Srinagar and Jammu (following the same 'Durbar Move' seasonal pattern as the wider UT administration, per Chapter 1) and a circuit bench arrangement covering Ladakh.

rows: Common HC for UT of J&K and UT of Ladakh
Direct applicability of all Central Acts

blocks.content: This shared-High-Court arrangement for two separate UTs (J&K and Ladakh) is structurally similar to a few other Indian shared-jurisdiction arrangements (such as the Punjab and Haryana High Court serving two states plus Chandigarh UT, or the Bombay High Court serving Maharashtra, Goa and other UTs) but is nonetheless a distinctive and specifically tested feature of the post-2019 J&K/Ladakh judicial landscape.

★ EXAM POINT: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh is a single, shared High Court for BOTH Union Territories created by the 2019 reorganisation — a frequently tested fact, since candidates sometimes incorrectly assume each new UT received its own separate court.

items: The J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 created a common High Court for the UT of Jammu & Kashmir and the UT of Ladakh.
Transition from the historic Ranbir Penal Code (RPC) to Indian statutory criminal codes is a frequently tested topic.
Historical establishment of the J&K High Court dates back to 1928 during Maharaja rule.

As detailed in Chapter 14, the erstwhile state's own separate legal codes — including the Ranbir Penal Code (the region's historic criminal code, itself modelled closely on the Indian Penal Code but maintained as a separate, J&K-specific enactment during the state era) — were repealed and replaced by the applicable central codes following the 2019 reorganisation.

This legal-code unification was a key practical effect of the broader constitutional reorganisation, bringing J&K's substantive and procedural criminal law fully in line with the rest of India for the first time since the Dogra-era codification of the Ranbir Penal Code.
High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh = the single, shared High Court for both post-2019 UTs, with seats at Srinagar and Jammu (Durbar Move pattern) and a Ladakh circuit bench.
Ranbir Penal Code (the historic, separate J&K criminal code) was repealed post-2019 and replaced by applicable central criminal codes.
